introduction-there-are-no-solutions-only.core: Engineering rarely has perfect answers, only trade-offs. Your job is to see what each option gains and gives up, decide which downsides you can tolerate, and choose deliberately.

first_principles.problem: Engineers hunt for 'the right answer' and get stuck, or pick the option with the best marketing. Every choice (database, platform, build vs buy) gains something and costs something.
truths: Every option has downsides.
Which downside is tolerable depends on context.
Undeliberate choices still trade something.
derivation: List what each option **gains** and **gives up**.
Decide which downsides your team **can tolerate**.
Choose and **record** why.

analogy.title: Buying a car
analogy.story: A sports car is fast but impractical; an SUV is roomy but thirsty. There's no best car, only the best car for your life.
analogy.breaks: Car specs are published. Software trade-offs often appear only after adoption, so seek experience reports.

example.title: Kubernetes or a simpler platform?
example.scenario: A 6-person team weighs Kubernetes vs a PaaS.

steps.label: Gains/costs
steps.detail: Kubernetes adds control but needs operations skill they lack.

example.outcome: a choice that fits the team, with a known revisit point.

check.q: What's your job when facing two options?
check.a: Identify each option's trade-offs, decide which downsides you can tolerate, and choose deliberately.

the-anatomy-of-a-trade-off.core: A true trade-off exists only when improving one quality necessarily degrades another. If an option is better on every axis, it isn't a trade-off, just a better approach.

first_principles.problem: Teams call everything a trade-off, even choices where one option simply dominates. Or they miss the real axes being traded (consistency vs latency, simplicity vs flexibility).
truths: Some improvements are free (dominant options).
Real trade-offs sit on recurring axes.
Naming the axis clarifies the choice.
derivation: Check for **dominance** first: is one option better on everything?
If not, name the **axes**: performance/cost, consistency/availability, simplicity/flexibility, speed/safety, control/convenience.
Place each option on those axes.

analogy.title: Designing a car
analogy.story: A bigger engine adds speed but also weight and fuel use; more steel adds safety but slows it. Those are real trade-offs. A better spark plug that improves everything isn't.
analogy.breaks: Car physics are fixed. In software, new technology sometimes removes old trade-offs, so re-check the axes.

example.title: Adding a read cache

steps.label: Axes
steps.detail: Latency vs consistency and operational complexity.

steps.label: Tolerance
steps.detail: Product pages tolerate 60 s staleness; balances don't.

example.outcome: the decision focuses on the axes that actually matter.

check.q: When is a choice not a trade-off?
check.a: When one option is better or equal on every axis that matters.

trade-off-1-simplicity-vs-flexibility.core: Every abstraction adds flexibility and costs simplicity. Build the simple thing for today's need, and generalise only when real second and third use cases appear.

first_principles.problem: To send one welcome email, an engineer builds a pluggable notification framework with providers, templates and channels. It takes weeks, confuses everyone and is never extended.
truths: Unused flexibility is pure cost.
Simple code is easier to change later.
Future needs are usually guessed wrong.
derivation: Start with the **simplest thing** that works.
Wait for the **rule of three** before abstracting.
Refactor to flexibility **when real needs arrive**.

analogy.title: Hammer vs multi-tool
analogy.story: A hammer does one job perfectly. A multi-tool does many jobs, but it's a terrible hammer.
analogy.breaks: Tools are bought. Software flexibility must also be maintained forever, so it costs every day.

example.title: The welcome email
example.scenario: Product asks for a sign-up email.

steps.label: Later
steps.detail: When SMS arrives, extract a small notifier interface.

example.outcome: the feature ships today, and flexibility arrives only when it earns its keep.

check.q: What's the risk of building flexibility early?
check.a: You pay complexity costs for cases that may never come, and usually guess the future shape wrong.

trade-off-2-buy-vs-build-vs-open-source.core: Build gives perfect fit and control but steals focus and carries forever-maintenance. Buy gives speed and support for money and lock-in. Open source sits between, costing your team's time to run it.

first_principles.problem: "We can build auth in two weeks" turns into years of password hashing, MFA, token handling and security patches, done by engineers not working on the product.
truths: Engineering time is the scarcest resource.
Non-core systems still need maintenance.
Vendors cost money and add dependency.
derivation: Ask: is this **core to our differentiation**?
Not core: **buy** (or managed open source).
Core and unmet by market: **build**.
Open source: free licence, **paid in operations time**.
Count **total cost of ownership** over 3 years.

analogy.title: Making your own furniture
analogy.story: A carpenter might build a dining table for joy, but nobody builds their own fridge. Build what you're uniquely good at; buy appliances.
analogy.breaks: A fridge doesn't need weekly security patches. Software you build does, forever.

example.title: Authentication for a SaaS app
example.scenario: Build in-house, use Auth0/Cognito, or run Keycloak?

steps.label: Core check
steps.detail: Auth isn't what customers pay for.

steps.label: TCO
steps.detail: Building needs MFA, recovery, audits forever.

example.outcome: engineers spend their time on what makes the product different.

points: OSS isn't free: you pay in time.

check.a: It's hard to get right, needs constant security upkeep, and rarely differentiates the product.

trade-off-3-vendor-lock-in-risk-assessme.core: Lock-in is the cost of leaving a vendor. It's not inherently bad: accept it consciously where the vendor's value is high and switching is unlikely, and limit it where leaving is plausible.

first_principles.problem: Teams either avoid all managed services (and rebuild everything) or adopt proprietary services everywhere, then can't respond to a 40% price rise.
truths: Deep integration delivers value and raises switching cost.
Abstraction layers cost effort and lose features.
Some vendors are more likely to change terms.
derivation: Estimate **switching cost** (data gravity, proprietary APIs, skills).
Estimate **likelihood you'd want to leave**.
High value, low exit likelihood: **embrace** the service.
Plausible exit: keep **portable boundaries** (standard formats, interfaces).

analogy.title: Buying a house in a one-employer town
analogy.story: The house may be perfect and cheap, but leaving that employer means selling and moving too. Fine, if you choose it knowingly.
analogy.breaks: Houses don't change price unilaterally. Vendors can, which is why you assess pricing risk too.

example.title: DynamoDB vs Postgres on RDS
example.scenario: A team weighs a proprietary DB against a portable one.

steps.label: Assessment
steps.detail: Postgres skills and data move anywhere.

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: Similar value, lower switching cost wins.

example.outcome: lock-in is taken on where it pays, not by accident.

points: Lock-in is a trade-off, not a sin.
Keep boundaries portable where exit is plausible.

check.a: When the vendor's value is high and the chance you'll need to leave is low.

trade-off-4-speed-vs-reliability-move-fa.core: Shipping fast and staying stable pull against each other. The right point depends on the cost of failure: a pre-launch startup and a payments platform should sit at very different places.

first_principles.problem: One-size policies fail both ways: a startup drowning in release ceremony, or a bank deploying straight to production.
truths: Failure cost varies hugely by product and stage.
Safety practices take time.
Some practices improve both (automation, small batches).
derivation: Estimate the **cost of an incident** (users, money, trust).
Pick safety practices proportionate to it: tests, canaries, staged rollouts, load tests.
Prefer practices that **improve both** (CI, small changes, fast rollback).

analogy.title: Driving speed by road
analogy.story: You drive fast on an empty motorway and slowly past a school. Same car, different risk.
analogy.breaks: Roads have signs. Your product's risk level must be judged and revisited as you grow.

example.title: Same feature, two companies
example.scenario: A photo-sharing beta and a payment processor ship similar changes.

steps.label: Beta
steps.detail: Bugs affect a few hundred friendly users.

steps.label: Payments
steps.detail: Bugs move real money, so canaries and approvals.

example.outcome: each team's safety investment matches its real risk.

check.q: Name a practice that improves both speed and reliability.
check.a: Small, frequent deploys with automated tests and fast rollback.

reversibility-the-hidden-dimension-of-ev.core: Every trade-off has a hidden fourth dimension: how easily you can undo it. Reversible choices deserve quick decisions; irreversible ones deserve deep analysis.

first_principles.problem: Teams analyse a testing-framework choice as deeply as a primary-database choice, or rush the database choice like a framework pick.
truths: Reversal costs vary from minutes to years.
Analysis time is limited.
Wrong but reversible is cheap.
derivation: Rate each option's **reversal cost**.
**Two-way door**: decide fast, learn by doing.
**One-way door**: analyse, prototype, consult.
Prefer options that **keep doors open** when unsure.

analogy.title: Renting before buying
analogy.story: Not sure about a neighbourhood? Rent first. It costs a bit more but keeps your options open.
analogy.breaks: Rent is a known premium. The price of reversibility in software (abstractions, flags) must be estimated.

example.title: Database vs test framework
example.scenario: Two decisions on the same day.

steps.label: Fast
steps.detail: Pick Vitest; swapping later is easy.

steps.label: Careful
steps.detail: Prototype two databases with real load.

example.outcome: analysis time goes where mistakes are expensive.

points: Reversibility changes how much analysis you need.

check.q: What's the most common mistake here?
check.a: Treating every decision as a one-way door, which creates committees and delay.

building-a-trade-off-analysis-framework.core: A repeatable five-step framework turns trade-off judgement into a team practice: define the decision precisely, name the axes, list options, score them against your constraints, and record the decision with its rationale.

first_principles.problem: Trade-off judgements in one person's head are fragile, hard to communicate and impossible to audit. Different people weigh things differently without knowing it.
truths: Precise questions get precise answers.
Explicit criteria reduce bias.
Written decisions can be revisited.
derivation: **1. Define** the decision in one precise sentence with constraints.
**2. Identify axes** (cost, ops burden, speed, lock-in).
**3. List options**, including 'do nothing'.
**4. Evaluate** each against the axes with evidence.
**5. Decide and record** (ADR), with a revisit trigger.

analogy.title: Judging a competition
analogy.story: Judges agree the criteria and weights before tasting, score each entry, and publish the scores, so the result can be explained and challenged.
analogy.breaks: Competition criteria are fixed. Engineering constraints change, so include a revisit trigger.

example.title: Choosing a CI/CD platform
example.scenario: 12 engineers, GitHub, Kubernetes on AWS, $500/month, low maintenance priority.

steps.label: Define
steps.detail: Precise constraints rule out options quickly.

steps.label: Record
steps.detail: ADR with a revisit at 30 engineers.

example.outcome: a defensible, shareable decision that can be revisited when constraints change.

check.q: Why include 'do nothing' as an option?
check.a: It sets a baseline cost and sometimes turns out to be the best trade-off.
